units.title: Be and Have Foundation
units.focus: Use be, have, and there is/are to introduce people, things, places, and basic situations.
objectives: Introduce yourself and other people with be.
Use have to talk about possession, family, and simple work items.
Use there is and there are to describe places and objects.

sections.title: Meaning
body: Use be for identity, age, feelings, jobs, and location.
Use have for possession, family, schedules, and things you use.
Use there is and there are to say that something exists in a place.

structures.example: I am a student.
She has a laptop.
There is a notebook on the desk.
They are not at home.
Are you ready?

mistakes.why: Do not use be before have when have means possession.
Use has with he, she, and it.
Use there is with one thing and there are with plural things.

examples.sentence: I am ready for class.
examples.note: Be describes a current state.

examples.sentence: She has two children.
examples.note: Has shows possession or family information.

examples.sentence: There is a laptop on the desk.
examples.note: There is introduces one object in a place.

examples.sentence: They are at home after school.
examples.note: Are links the subject to a location.

units.title: Present Simple Foundation
units.focus: Use Present Simple for habits, routines, facts, and schedules.
objectives: Recognize when Present Simple is the right tense.
Build affirmative, negative, and question forms.
Avoid the common he/she/it -s mistake.

sections.title: Meaning
body: Present Simple describes habits, routines, general truths, permanent situations, and schedules.
It usually answers the question: what do you usually do?

structures.pattern: Subject + base verb (+ s/es for he/she/it)
structures.example: He works as an IT engineer.
He does not work on Sundays.
Does he work in IT?

mistakes.why: He/she/it needs -s in affirmative Present Simple.

mistakes.wrong: He does not works on Sundays.
mistakes.right: He does not work on Sundays.
mistakes.why: Does already carries the third-person marker, so the main verb returns to base form.

examples.note: This describes a regular work routine.

examples.note: Every morning signals a repeated habit.

examples.note: Every Tuesday shows a regular schedule.

examples.note: On Fridays points to a repeated family routine.

examples.sentence: We book a hotel before every vacation.
examples.note: Before every vacation describes a repeated travel habit.

units.title: Personal Information and Basic Questions
units.focus: Ask and answer basic personal questions about name, origin, job, family, and daily life.
objectives: Ask simple personal questions with be, do, and wh- words.
Answer basic questions about identity, origin, work, and family.
Use short polite questions in everyday introductions.

sections.title: Meaning
body: Use personal questions to start simple conversations and exchange basic information.
Use be questions for identity, origin, age, job, and location.
Use do questions for habits, routines, and simple daily actions.

structures.example: Where are you from?
What do you do every morning?
I am from Colombia.
I work in IT.
She does not work on Sundays.

mistakes.why: In be questions, put am/is/are before the subject.
Use do as the main verb for job questions, and keep the base form after do.
After does, the main verb returns to the base form.

sections.title: Meaning
body: Present Continuous describes actions happening now or around now.
It also describes temporary situations and current arrangements.

Use the -ing form after am, is, or are.

units.title: Present Perfect Experiences

sections.title: Meaning
body: Present Perfect connects a past action to now.
Use it for experiences, recent results, and completed actions when the exact time is not important.

structures.example: She has finished the report.
They have not visited the office yet.
Have you ever traveled for work?

mistakes.why: Present Perfect needs the past participle.
Use Simple Past with a finished time like yesterday.

examples.sentence: I have already sent the update.
examples.note: Already shows a completed result connected to now.

examples.sentence: We have visited that hotel before.
examples.note: Before points to an experience.

examples.sentence: She has not finished breakfast yet.
examples.note: Yet is common in negative Present Perfect.

units.title: Past, Future and Conditional Foundation
units.focus: Use time markers and sequence markers to choose and build past, future, and conditional forms.

sections.title: Meaning and usage
body: Past forms describe actions before now and usually need clear time order.
Future forms are used for plans, predictions, and formal expectations.
Conditional forms describe possible situations and hypothetical outcomes.
Perfect and continuous forms help show results and ongoing duration.
